claims.text: A nanostructured tungsten-based refractory-metal substrate with a thin carbide or nitride coating will have increased HER and HOR catalytic activity relative to standard bulk materials.
The coated, nanostructured tungsten substrate will have enhanced durability relative to standard bulk materials.
Nanostructuring increases the density of catalytically active sites.
A robust carbide or nitride surface layer improves electrochemical stability by protecting the substrate.
The proposed substrate is a dense tungsten-based refractory metal, potentially containing minor alloy additions.
The proposed nanoporous surface has 20–40% porosity.
The proposed nanoporous features are tens to hundreds of nanometers in size.
The proposed carbide or nitride coating is uniform and tens of nanometers thick.
The nanoporous architecture provides high surface area and increased active-site density.
The thin carbide or nitride layer provides structural and chemical stability under harsh electrochemical conditions.
High surface area from nanoscale porosity produces superior catalytic performance toward hydrogen reactions.
A chemically stable tungsten carbide or nitride layer mitigates surface degradation and thereby improves durability.
The modified electrodes will exhibit reduced HER and HOR overpotentials relative to unstructured or uncoated tungsten-based electrodes.
The modified electrodes will exhibit improved HER and HOR current density relative to unstructured or uncoated tungsten-based electrodes.
The modified electrodes will have a longer operational lifetime than unstructured or uncoated tungsten-based electrodes.
Loss of substrate or coating integrity at extremely high temperatures or under exceedingly corrosive conditions may reduce the proposed activity and durability improvements.

The hypothesis is invalidated if the modified electrodes fail to show both significantly better stability and at least 20–50% higher current density at comparable overpotentials than the unstructured or uncoated baseline.
